## Italy is curtailing record amounts of solar, here's why.


**Italy hit 46.6 GW of installed PV by June 2026, after adding 3.1 GW in just the first half of the year. Storage is scaling too, past 19.3 GWh** . On paper, this is exactly what a fast-growing solar market should look like.


Off paper, something else is happening. In 2025, **Italy curtailed 162 GWh of solar generation** that plants were ready to produce but the grid couldn’t take. That’s more than **20 times what was curtailed in 2024.** And the trend hasn’t eased: **preliminary data puts spring 2026 alone at 182 GWh, more than the whole of 2025.**


Period Curtailed PV generation


2024 (full year) 7.5 GWh


2025 (full year) 162 GWh


Spring 2026 (one season) 182 GWh


So two numbers are now moving in opposite directions at once. More solar gets connected every month. A shrinking share of what it produces actually reaches somewhere.


## When nothing is actually broken


A curtailed plant and an underperforming plant can look identical on a production chart. Modules are producing, inverters are available, **nothing has failed, and the energy still doesn’t reach the grid** . In 2025, that gap split into three distinct causes:


Cause GWh Share


Generation exceeded grid absorption capacity 64 40%


Grid congestion 58 36%


Planned infrastructure works 38 24%


None of those point to equipment that needs fixing. **They point to constraints sitting outside the plant entirely,** which is exactly what makes them easy to miss in a standard monitoring report.


## A problem with a postcode


Curtailment isn’t spread evenly across the country. **Centro-Sud** **carried 101 GWh** of the 2025 total, 62% of it, despite the region holding nowhere near 62% of installed capacity nationally.


Zone Share of 2025 curtailment Share of installed PV capacity


Centro-Sud 62% ~52%


Rest of Italy (North) 38% ~48%


A portfolio weighted toward Centro-Sud is carrying meaningfully more curtailment exposure than national averages suggest, and **that’s the kind of risk that only shows up once the numbers are broken down by region.**


## Too many causes to check by hand


> Layer that regional variation on top of the three causes above, add **inverter faults, string issues, weather and degradation** , and a single production gap can have a long list of possible explanations.
>
>
> Checking every one by hand across a 46.6 GW national fleet, or even one growing portfolio, isn’t realistic. The useful question stops being “was production low” and becomes **how much was lost, why, and whether anything could have been done about it.**


## Where storage comes in, and a tender behind it


Sited next to curtailed solar, a battery can absorb energy the grid won’t take and release it later, turning a loss into a delay instead **. Italy already has 19.3 GWh of storage installed,** and the push to add more now has a specific date attached to it.


Terna’s storage capacity auction, **MACSE** , awarded its first round in October 2025, mostly to state-backed players. Terna has also proposed cutting battery de-rating in the 2026 capacity market, a change that would tighten qualified capacity and could push clearing prices higher still.


None of that pays off on its own. **A battery that sits next to a plant but isn’t managed with it doesn’t solve curtailment, it just adds a second asset to monitor separately.** Solar output, grid conditions, available storage, state of charge and energy actually delivered have to be read as one picture before any of this reduces real losses.

**“Production is 8% below expected”** isn’t an answer on its own. It’s where the real question starts: was that 8% a curtailment order, an inverter fault, a string problem, or just weather, and what did each piece actually cost in kWh and in euros?

## Small losses that compound as the fleet grows


162 GWh was still only about


**0.4%** of Italy’s annual solar output in 2025,


so this isn’t a fleet-wide crisis. It is a cost that compounds: a few hours of curtailment here, a grid constraint there, a battery that wasn’t dispatched in time. None of those show up as one dramatic number. Across a growing portfolio, they add up fast anyway.


> The next phase of Italian solar isn’t only about how many megawatts get installed. It’s about how well the ones already connected are actually being used.

## Frequently Asked Questions


Why is Italy curtailing solar energy, and what does it mean for plant owners?


**Italy’s growing solar capacity** can put pressure on the electricity grid when generation exceeds what the grid can accommodate in a particular location or at a particular time. For plant owners, this can mean lost generation and potential revenue, even when their equipment is working correctly


. Understanding when curtailment occurs and how much energy is affected is the first step towards evaluating possible solutions.


Can battery energy storage systems (BESS) help solar plants avoid curtailment?


**Yes,[BESS](https://smarthelio.com/bess-analytics-for-solar-storage/) can help reduce certain forms of curtailment by storing surplus solar electricity and releasing it when conditions are more favourable.** However, the benefit depends on battery capacity, grid connection constraints, charging permissions and the plant’s operating strategy. Storage is not a universal solution, so asset owners need to understand their curtailment patterns before deciding whether a battery makes sense.
[Know more about BESS](https://smarthelio.com/bess-analytics-for-solar-storage/)


How can solar asset owners determine whether investing in BESS is financially worthwhile?


Asset owners should evaluate **how much energy is being curtailed, when it occurs, the potential value of shifting that energy, and the costs of installing and operating a battery.** Battery degradation, market prices, grid restrictions and available revenue streams also affect the business case. The goal is to determine whether **the potential benefits justify the investment,** rather than assuming that every curtailed megawatt-hour can be recovered.


How can operators distinguish grid curtailment from technical losses at a solar plant?


Grid curtailment occurs when available generation is restricted by grid or system conditions, while **technical losses may result from equipment faults, inverter underperformance or other plant inefficiencies.** Operators can investigate the difference by comparing generation data, export limitations, inverter behaviour and operational records. **[SmartHelio’s](https://smarthelio.com/book-a-demo/) analytics can help identify underperformance and investigate operational issues** , supporting a clearer understanding of where action may be needed.


What should operators monitor when managing a solar plant and its battery storage system?


Operators should monitor **solar generation, energy flows, battery state of charge (SOC), state of health (SOH), charging and discharging behaviour, and operational constraints.** Looking at these factors together helps teams understand how the solar plant and battery are performing, identify potential issues and **make better-informed operating decisions.**[SmartHelio](https://smarthelio.com/) supports[solar and BESS monitoring and analysi](https://smarthelio.com/solar-and-bess-co-optimization-how-it-improves-project-profitability/) s, helping operators investigate performance across their assets.
